Interpolative Separable Density-Fitting for Transcorrelated Hamiltonians

Ke Liao Email: ke.liao.whu@gmail.com Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research, Heisenbergstrasse 1, 70569 Stuttgart, Germany Affiliation: Department of Chemistry, Yale University, Sterling Chemistry Laboratory, 225 Prospect St, New Haven, CT 06511, USA    Yifan Cheng Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research, Heisenbergstrasse 1, 70569 Stuttgart, Germany    Werner Dobrautz Affiliation: Center for Advanced Systems Understanding (CASUS), Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), 02826 Görlitz, Germany Affiliation: Center for Scalable Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence (ScaDS.AI), TU Dresden, 01062 Dresden, Germany    Tianyu Zhu Email: tianyu.zhu@yale.edu Affiliation: Department of Chemistry, Yale University, Sterling Chemistry Laboratory, 225 Prospect St, New Haven, CT 06511, USA    Ali Alavi Email: a.alavi@fkf.mpg.de Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research, Heisenbergstrasse 1, 70569 Stuttgart, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The transcorrelated (TC) method folds a Jastrow correlator into the Hamiltonian by similarity transformation, building the electron–electron cusp into the effective interaction and thereby dramatically accelerating the convergence of correlated calculations toward the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. We make this framework practical for large systems and flexible, multi-center correlators by compressing the grid-evaluated TC integrals with the interpolative separable density-fitting (ISDF) approximation, combined with the effective two-body (xTC) treatment of the three-body operator. This low-rank representation reduces storage and integration costs by orders of magnitude, and a multi-GPU implementation with automatic differentiation of the correlator makes the construction routine for large basis sets. We demonstrate the resulting ISDF-xTC-CCSD method on the linear hydrogen chain, reaching the joint thermodynamic and CBS limits with basis sets up to cc-pV5Z in agreement with state-of-the-art many-body references to within about 1 mHa/atom, and on the benzene ground-state energy with up to 1200 orbitals (cc-pCV5Z), where the method attains state-of-the-art accuracy at the coupled cluster singles and doubles level and its CBS extrapolation is markedly more robust than that of conventional coupled-cluster methods.

I Introduction

The accurate treatment of electron correlation is the central challenge of ab initio electronic structure theory, and a major practical obstacle is the slow convergence of correlated energies with the size of the one-particle basis. Because an antisymmetric product of smooth orbitals cannot reproduce the cusp in the wavefunction as two electrons coalesce, correlation energies converge only as 𝒪⁡(X−3)\mathcal{O}(X^{-3}) in the cardinal number XX of a correlation-consistent basis set[28, 23], so that reaching the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit with orbital-product expansions alone demands prohibitively large bases.

A well-established route around this bottleneck is to build the electron–electron cusp directly into the wavefunction. Explicitly correlated R12 and F12 methods augment the orbital expansion with terms that depend explicitly on the interelectronic distance r12r_{12}, restoring the cusp and accelerating basis-set convergence by roughly two cardinal numbers[29, 27, 19]. These methods deliver near-CBS correlation energies in modest bases, but require specialized many-electron integrals and are tailored to particular correlation-method implementations. A complementary strategy, pursued here, folds the correlation factor into the Hamiltonian itself rather than the wavefunction.

The transcorrelated (TC) method, originally introduced by Boys and Handy[8, 5, 7, 4, 6], realizes this idea. Similarity transforming the Hamiltonian with a Jastrow factor, H¯=F−1​H^​F\bar{H}=F^{-1}\hat{H}F with F=eτ^F=e^{\hat{\tau}}, builds the electron–electron cusp and other correlation effects directly into the Hamiltonian, markedly accelerating basis-set convergence and extending the reach of low-order coupled-cluster approximations into strongly correlated regimes. The price is that the transcorrelated Hamiltonian acquires, beyond the usual two-body interaction, an additional effective two-body term and a genuine three-body operator, whose explicit (rank-six) treatment is prohibitive beyond small systems. Interest in the method has grown steadily across several groups and correlation treatments. Tsuneyuki and co-workers pioneered its application to solids, coupling the correlator optimization to variational Monte Carlo and developing efficient plane-wave algorithms and correlated band structures[56, 48, 43, 42]. Alavi and co-workers combined the TC method with full configuration-interaction quantum Monte Carlo[35, 20], coupled-cluster theory[32, 50, 49], and the density-matrix renormalization group[33], developed systematic Jastrow-factor optimizations[21, 15], and introduced the effective transcorrelated (xTC) scheme[32, 10, 26], which removes the three-body bottleneck by contracting the three-body operator with the reference one-particle density matrix into an effective two-body correction, restoring the formal scaling of a conventional two-body method. Reiher and co-workers formulated transcorrelated matrix-product operators and non-iterative triples corrections[2, 40]; Ten-no introduced a nonunitary projective transcorrelation inspired by the F12 ansatz[55]; and Giner and co-workers constructed inexpensive three-body correlation factors with analytic integrals[18, 1]. These developments have been applied to atoms and small molecules[16], the uniform electron gas and periodic solids[35, 32, 52], and even quantum-computing hardware[12]—but almost always for relatively small systems.

Scaling the transcorrelated method to larger systems exposes a second, less widely appreciated bottleneck: the evaluation of the transcorrelated two-body integrals themselves. For simple correlators these can be obtained analytically[18, 1, 2], but analytic schemes are correlator-specific and become cumbersome—or intractable—for the flexible, multi-center correlators, such as the Boys–Handy[6] or Drummond–Towler–Needs[14] forms, that are needed to capture electron–electron, electron–nucleus, and three-body electron–electron–nucleus correlation simultaneously. Numerical real-space integration is fully general and correlator-agnostic, but its naive cost is prohibitive: evaluating the transcorrelated two-body integrals requires a double sum over grid points for every orbital pair, scaling as 𝒪⁡(Ng2​Norb2)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}^{2}N_{\rm orb}^{2}) in the number of grid points NgN_{g}; explicit evaluation of the full three-body (rank-six) integrals is more expensive still; and even after the xTC contraction eliminates the explicit three-body tensor, the assembly of the effective two-body correction—the dominant cost in practice—couples the same double grid sums to 𝒪⁡(Ng​Norb4)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}N_{\rm orb}^{4}) orbital-pair contractions. None of these costs is affordable for production calculations without further factorization.

We address this bottleneck with the interpolative separable density-fitting (ISDF) approximation[34, 25, 45], which compresses products of orbitals (and orbital gradients) on a real-space grid into a low-rank representation anchored at a small set of interpolation points, and which has accelerated density fitting[34, 45], hybrid density-functional theory and exact exchange in molecules and solids[25, 13, 58, 47], G​WGW and random-phase-approximation calculations[17, 60, 61], post-Hartree–Fock methods[24, 31, 37, 38, 36], quantum embedding and local correlation in crystalline materials[59], and compact Hamiltonian representations for quantum computing[30]. We show that the transcorrelated two-body (KK) and effective two-body (xTC, Δ​U\Delta U) integrals inherit this low-rank structure, and we build them for a general differentiable Jastrow factor whose gradients are obtained by automatic differentiation, eliminating the need for hand-coded, correlator-specific integral routines.

This work contributes: (i) an ISDF factorization of the transcorrelated KK and Δ​U\Delta U integrals for a general grid-evaluated correlator, with a pivoted-Cholesky selection of interpolation points that is independent of the Jastrow; (ii) a GPU-compatible Jastrow-optimization workflow that combines the reference-variance VMC objective of Ref. 21—complementary to recent deterministic Jastrow-optimization schemes[15]—with automatic-differentiation gradients and Polyak–Ruppert parameter averaging; (iii) a GPU-accelerated producer/consumer pipeline with multi-GPU dispatch support and out-of-core storage that accelerates both the ISDF integral construction and the downstream CCSD solver, keeping the approach tractable for up to 1200 orbitals in large basis sets; and (iv) integration with a restricted CCSD solver for non-Hermitian transcorrelated integrals, building on earlier transcorrelated coupled-cluster work[32, 50, 49]. We validate the ISDF approximation on two benchmarks: the linear hydrogen chain, where transcorrelation accelerates basis-set convergence and the thermodynamic-limit energies agree with state-of-the-art AFQMC+Δ\DeltaDMRG references[41] to within 11 mHa/atom, and the benzene molecule, where the construction remains tractable up to the cc-pCV5Z basis (Norb=1200N_{\rm orb}=1200).

II Theoretical Framework

II.1 Transcorrelation theory

The transcorrelated Hamiltonian is obtained by a similarity transformation of the bare electronic Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} in first quantization:

H¯=F−1​H^​F,F=eτ^,\bar{H}=F^{-1}\,\hat{H}\,F,\qquad F=e^{\hat{\tau}}, (1)

where FF is the Jastrow factor and τ^\hat{\tau} is the Jastrow operator. The production correlator contains a one-electron nuclear-cusp term χ⁡(𝐫)\chi({\bf r}) [21] and a symmetric two-electron term u2​(𝐫i,𝐫j)u_{2}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j}). For a fixed NN-electron system these combine into a single symmetric effective pair kernel,

u⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)\displaystyle u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j}) =u2​(𝐫i,𝐫j)+χ⁡(𝐫i)+χ⁡(𝐫j)N−1,\displaystyle=u_{2}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})+\frac{\chi({\bf r}_{i})+\chi({\bf r}_{j})}{N-1}, (2)
τ^\displaystyle\hat{\tau} =∑iNχ⁡(𝐫i)+∑i<jNu2​(𝐫i,𝐫j)=∑i<jNu⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)\displaystyle=\sum_{i}^{N}\chi({\bf r}_{i})+\sum_{i<j}^{N}u_{2}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})=\sum_{i<j}^{N}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})
=12∑i≠jNu(𝐫i,𝐫j),F(𝐑)=∏i<jeu⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}^{N}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j}),\qquad F({\bf R})=\prod_{i<j}e^{u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})},

where the second equality holds because each electron label appears in exactly N−1N-1 ordered pairs, so the 1/(N−1)1/(N-1) factor in uu resums the one-body term exactly. The one-body factor is thereby represented exactly within the same pair-product form used by the integral kernels. The effective uu is real-valued and symmetric, u⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)=u⁡(𝐫j,𝐫i)u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})=u({\bf r}_{j},{\bf r}_{i}), and collects the one-electron nuclear-cusp correction together with the electron–electron, electron–nucleus, and three-body electron–electron–nucleus contributions in u2u_{2}. In the expansion below, 𝒫⁡(𝐫i1,…,𝐫in)\mathcal{P}({\bf r}_{i_{1}},\dots,{\bf r}_{i_{n}}) denotes the symmetrizer over the electron coordinates listed as its arguments, i.e. the sum over all n!n! permutations of the nn electron labels.

Expanding H¯\bar{H} via the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula, and using the fact that τ^\hat{\tau} depends only on the electron positions and contains no gradient or integral operators, the series terminates at the second commutator and produces at most three-body operators:

H¯\displaystyle\bar{H} =H^+[H^,τ^]+12​[[H^,τ^],τ^]\displaystyle=\hat{H}+[\hat{H},\hat{\tau}]+\tfrac{1}{2}[[\hat{H},\hat{\tau}],\hat{\tau}] (3)
=H^−∑i<j𝒫⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)​[12​∇i2u​(𝐫i,𝐫j)+12​(∇iu​(𝐫i,𝐫j))2+∇iu​(𝐫i,𝐫j)⋅∇i]\displaystyle=\hat{H}-\sum_{i<j}\mathcal{P}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla_{i}^{2}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})+\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\nabla_{i}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})\big)^{2}+\nabla_{i}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})\cdot\nabla_{i}\right]
−∑i<j<k𝒫(𝐫i,𝐫j,𝐫k)∇iu(𝐫i,𝐫j)⋅∇iu(𝐫i,𝐫k).\displaystyle-\sum_{i<j<k}\mathcal{P}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j},{\bf r}_{k})\,\nabla_{i}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})\cdot\nabla_{i}u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{k}).

Projected onto a set of one-electron orbitals {ϕp}\{\phi_{p}\}, H¯\bar{H} assumes the second-quantized form

H¯=\displaystyle\bar{H}={} hp​q​ap†​aq+12​(Vr​sp​q−Kr​sp​q)​ap†​aq†​as​ar\displaystyle h_{pq}\,a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,(V^{pq}_{rs}-K^{pq}_{rs})\,a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{s}a_{r} (4)
−16​Ls​t​up​q​r​ap†​aq†​ar†​au​at​as,\displaystyle-\tfrac{1}{6}\,L^{pqr}_{stu}\,a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{r}^{\dagger}a_{u}a_{t}a_{s},

where the Einstein summation convention is used. The two-body KK and three-body LL corrections are

Kr​sp​q\displaystyle K^{pq}_{rs} =𝒫^12​[⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)|12​∇12u​(1,2)+12​(∇1u​(1,2))2+∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1|ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)⟩],\displaystyle=\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\!\left[\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)|\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla_{1}^{2}u(1,2)+\tfrac{1}{2}(\nabla_{1}u(1,2))^{2}+\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}|\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)}\right], (5)
Ls​t​up​q​r\displaystyle L^{pqr}_{stu} =𝒫^123​⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)​ϕr​(3)|∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1u​(1,3)|ϕs​(1)​ϕt​(2)​ϕu​(3)⟩,\displaystyle=\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{123}\,\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)\phi_{r}(3)|\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}u(1,3)|\phi_{s}(1)\phi_{t}(2)\phi_{u}(3)},

with the shorthand ϕp​(i)≡ϕp​(𝐫i)\phi_{p}(i)\equiv\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{i}) and u⁡(i,j)≡u⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)u(i,j)\equiv u({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j}).

II.2 Jastrow correlator used in this work

We use the flexible multi-center Boys–Handy (BH) correlator[6], which captures electron–electron, electron–nucleus, and three-body electron–electron–nucleus correlation, with its linear and nonlinear parameters optimized by variational Monte Carlo (VMC). The BH form is written not in terms of the bare interparticle distances but in terms of bounded, monotone scaled distances

r¯i​I=bI​ri​I1+bI​ri​I,r¯i​j=d​ri​j1+d​ri​j,\bar{r}_{iI}\;=\;\frac{b_{I}\,r_{iI}}{1+b_{I}\,r_{iI}},\qquad\bar{r}_{ij}\;=\;\frac{d\,r_{ij}}{1+d\,r_{ij}}, (6)

with 𝐫i​I=𝐫i−𝐑I{\bf r}_{iI}={\bf r}_{i}-{\bf R}_{I}, ri​I=|𝐫i​I|r_{iI}=|{\bf r}_{iI}|, ri​j=|𝐫i−𝐫j|r_{ij}=|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}|, and variational scale parameters bI>0b_{I}>0 (nucleus-resolved) and d>0d>0. The scaled variables satisfy r¯∈[0,1)\bar{r}\in[0,1), so that monomials r¯m\bar{r}^{m} remain bounded at long range, and all positive integer powers can be mixed without divergence. The correlator reads

u2​(𝐫i,𝐫j)=∑I∑kckI​[r¯i​Imk​r¯j​Ink+r¯j​Imk​r¯i​Ink]​r¯i​jok,u_{2}({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})=\sum_{I}\sum_{k}c_{k}^{I}\,\Big[\bar{r}_{iI}^{m_{k}}\,\bar{r}_{jI}^{n_{k}}+\bar{r}_{jI}^{m_{k}}\,\bar{r}_{iI}^{n_{k}}\Big]\,\bar{r}_{ij}^{o_{k}}, (7)

where (mk,nk,ok)(m_{k},n_{k},o_{k}) are user-chosen non-negative-integer exponents and ckIc_{k}^{I} are the linear variational coefficients. A dedicated term with mk=nk=0m_{k}=n_{k}=0 and ok=1o_{k}=1 is retained in a cusp-normalized form, with its masked prefactor fixed so that the summed short-range slope satisfies the opposite-spin electron–electron Kato condition, ∂u2/∂ri​j|ri​j→0=1/2\partial u_{2}/\partial r_{ij}|_{r_{ij}\to 0}=1/2. The same spin-independent two-electron correlator u2u_{2} is applied to every electron pair, so it satisfies the opposite-spin Kato cusp exactly but does not separately impose the same-spin cusp condition (14\tfrac{1}{4}); all systems studied here are closed-shell. The remaining ckIc_{k}^{I}, together with the nonlinear scale parameters dd and bIb_{I}, are optimized freely by VMC. The one-electron term χ\chi is the nuclear-cusp factor of Ref. 21; the composite correlator used in production is specified in the Computational Details. All correlator derivatives entering the integral kernels are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation, which is robust to arbitrary monomial degrees (mk,nk,ok)(m_{k},n_{k},o_{k}).

II.3 Variance optimization of the correlator by variational Monte Carlo

The linear coefficients {ckI}\{c_{k}^{I}\} and the nonlinear scale parameters {bI,d}\{b_{I},d\} in Eqs. (6)–(7) are optimized by variational Monte Carlo prior to the TC integral construction. Following the reference-variance approach of Ref. 21, which has been shown to optimize transcorrelated correlators more reliably than energy minimization, we minimize the variance of the local energy of the Slater–Jastrow trial wavefunction ΨT​(𝐑)=F⁡(𝐑)​Φ0​(𝐑)\Psi_{T}({\bf R})=F({\bf R})\,\Phi_{0}({\bf R}), with Φ0\Phi_{0} the Hartree–Fock reference determinant.

Sampling from the reference determinant.

A distinctive feature of the reference-variance protocol[21] is that Monte Carlo configurations are drawn from the reference density |Φ0​(𝐑)|2|\Phi_{0}({\bf R})|^{2} rather than from the Slater–Jastrow density |ΨT​(𝐑)|2|\Psi_{T}({\bf R})|^{2}. The sampling distribution is therefore held fixed throughout the parameter update and only the local energy

Eloc​(𝐑,𝜽)=H^​ΨT​(𝐑)ΨT​(𝐑),E_{\rm loc}({\bf R};\bm{\theta})\;=\;\frac{\hat{H}\,\Psi_{T}({\bf R})}{\Psi_{T}({\bf R})}, (8)

depends on the Jastrow parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} through the trial wavefunction ΨT\Psi_{T}, with the transcorrelated Hamiltonian H¯​(𝜽)\bar{H}({\bm{\theta}}) given by Eq. (3). This fixed sampling distribution has two operational advantages: the sampler need not be re-equilibrated after each parameter update, and the walker state stores only Slater matrices and their inverses. These are updated at cost 𝒪⁡(Nel2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm el}^{2}) per proposal (see Supporting Information Section ), while the Jastrow enters only through ElocE_{\rm loc} and never through the Metropolis acceptance ratio.

Objective function.

Concretely, at optimization step ss we sample NwN_{w} walker positions {𝐑k(s)}k=1Nw\{{\bf R}_{k}^{(s)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{w}} from |Φ0|2|\Phi_{0}|^{2}. Holding this batch fixed, write Ek​(𝜽)=Eloc​(𝐑k(s),𝜽)E_{k}(\bm{\theta})=E_{\rm loc}({\bf R}_{k}^{(s)};\bm{\theta}) and define its raw mean and mean absolute deviation (MAD) as

ms​(𝜽)\displaystyle m_{s}(\bm{\theta}) =1Nw​∑kEk​(𝜽),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{k}E_{k}(\bm{\theta}), (9)
ds​(𝜽)\displaystyle d_{s}(\bm{\theta}) =1Nw​∑k|Ek​(𝜽)−ms​(𝜽)|.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{k}\left|E_{k}(\bm{\theta})-m_{s}(\bm{\theta})\right|.

For outlier protection, each local energy is clipped to the interval set by the raw mean and MAD,

E~k​(𝜽)=clip⁡(CLOSEEk​(𝜽),ms​(𝜽)−5​ds​(𝜽),OPENms​(𝜽)+5​ds​(𝜽)).\begin{split}\widetilde{E}_{k}(\bm{\theta})=\operatorname{clip}\!\big(&E_{k}(\bm{\theta}),m_{s}(\bm{\theta})-5d_{s}(\bm{\theta}),\\ &m_{s}(\bm{\theta})+5d_{s}(\bm{\theta})\big).\end{split} (10)

The mean is then recomputed from the clipped energies, and the fixed-batch objective is

E~¯s​(𝜽)\displaystyle\overline{\widetilde{E}}_{s}(\bm{\theta}) =1Nw​∑kE~k​(𝜽),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{k}\widetilde{E}_{k}(\bm{\theta}), (11)
σs2​(𝜽)\displaystyle\sigma_{s}^{2}(\bm{\theta}) =1Nw−1​∑k[E~k​(𝜽)−E~¯s​(𝜽)]2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{w}-1}\sum_{k}\left[\widetilde{E}_{k}(\bm{\theta})-\overline{\widetilde{E}}_{s}(\bm{\theta})\right]^{2}.

No external reference energy enters the objective. The update in Eq. (12) evaluates the gradient of Eq. (11) at 𝜽(s)\bm{\theta}^{(s)}. The variance of Eq. (11) vanishes only if Φ0\Phi_{0} is an exact (right) eigenstate of H¯​(𝜽)\bar{H}(\bm{\theta}); within the finite Boys–Handy parameterization the optimizer instead seeks the lowest attainable variance, approaching this zero-variance principle to the extent that the correlator can absorb the transcorrelated Hamiltonian into the reference determinant.

Newton optimizer with Gauss–Newton curvature.

Because the objective Eq. (11) has the structure of a sum of squared residuals rk​(𝜽)=E~k​(𝜽)−E~¯s​(𝜽)r_{k}(\bm{\theta})=\widetilde{E}_{k}(\bm{\theta})-\overline{\widetilde{E}}_{s}(\bm{\theta}), we use a Newton-type update with Gauss–Newton curvature,

Ci​j​[𝜽]\displaystyle C_{ij}[\bm{\theta}] =1Nw​∑k=1Nw(∂θirk)​(∂θjrk)+λ​δi​j,\displaystyle=\;\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{w}}\big(\partial_{\theta_{i}}r_{k}\big)\!\big(\partial_{\theta_{j}}r_{k}\big)\;+\;\lambda\,\delta_{ij}, (12)
Δ​𝜽\displaystyle\Delta\bm{\theta} =−η​C−1​∇𝜽σs2,\displaystyle=\;-\,\eta\,C^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\sigma_{s}^{2},

with an adaptive Tikhonov shift λ\lambda and an exact Cholesky-based solve of the linear system. Gauss–Newton matches the quadratic structure of Eq. (11) near the optimum and converges in far fewer steps than plain stochastic gradient descent.

Optimization schedule.

The two-stage warm-up/refinement optimization schedule and the Polyak–Ruppert parameter averaging used to define the production correlator are described in Supporting Information Section .

II.4 Interpolative Separable Density-Fitting

The integration grid underlying the ISDF factorization is a Becke-partitioned atomic grid[3] with Treutler–Ahlrichs radial nodes, Lebedev angular grids, and Bragg–Slater radii, yielding points {𝐫g}g=1Ng\{{\bf r}_{g}\}_{g=1}^{N_{g}} and weights {wg}\{w_{g}\} that absorb the nuclear partitioning and radial Jacobian. We use PySCF grid level 2 throughout, as in Ref. 21.

Low-rank structure.

The approximation relies on a compact representation of orbital products. The pointwise Coulomb kernel itself is not low rank on the grid, but the contracted four-index tensor inherits low rank from the orbital overlap density

ρqp​(𝐫)≡ϕp​(𝐫)​ϕq​(𝐫),\rho^{p}_{q}({\bf r})\equiv\phi_{p}({\bf r})\,\phi_{q}({\bf r}), (13)

because rank⁡(A​B)≤min⁡[rank⁡(A),rank⁡(B)]\mathrm{rank}(AB)\leq\min[\mathrm{rank}(A),\mathrm{rank}(B)]. The same argument guarantees that the transcorrelated integrals KK and LL admit a low-rank representation of rank at most NμN_{\mu}, where NμN_{\mu} is the numerical rank of ρqp​(𝐫)\rho^{p}_{q}({\bf r}) on the chosen grid.

Pivot selection by pivoted Cholesky.

We select the scalar-channel interpolation points {𝐫μ(ϕ)}μ=1Nμ(ϕ)\{{\bf r}^{(\phi)}_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{N_{\mu}^{(\phi)}} by an iterative pivoted Cholesky decomposition (rather than by QR-column-pivoting[34, 25] or kk-means[13] as in previous ISDF implementations), in the spirit of the pivoted-Cholesky grid-point selection introduced for least-squares tensor hypercontraction[39]. Fusing the orbital indices into a single row index p​qpq and indexing the grid points by the column, the overlap-density matrix M(p​q),g=ϕp​(𝐫g)​ϕq​(𝐫g)M_{(pq),g}=\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{g}) has the separable Gram

(M⊤​M)g​g′\displaystyle(M^{\top}M)_{gg^{\prime}} =(∑pϕp​(𝐫g)​ϕp​(𝐫g′))2,\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{p}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\Big)^{2}, (14)
Dg(ϕ)≡(M⊤​M)g​g\displaystyle D^{(\phi)}_{g}\equiv(M^{\top}M)_{gg} =(∑pϕp​(𝐫g)2)2,\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{p}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})^{2}\Big)^{2},

which avoids ever forming the Norb2×NgN_{\rm orb}^{2}\times N_{g} matrix MM explicitly. In the actual quadrature implementation the pivot selection is performed on the weight-scaled orbitals ϕpw​(𝐫g)=wg1/2​ϕp​(𝐫g)\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g})=w_{g}^{1/2}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g}), so the scalar Cholesky matrix is

Sg​g′(ϕ)\displaystyle S^{(\phi)}_{gg^{\prime}} =(∑pϕpw​(𝐫g)​ϕpw​(𝐫g′))2,\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{p}\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\Big)^{2}, (15)
Dg(ϕ)\displaystyle D^{(\phi)}_{g} =wg2​(∑pϕp​(𝐫g)2)2.\displaystyle=w_{g}^{2}\Big(\sum_{p}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})^{2}\Big)^{2}.

Because the two-body K(1)K^{(1)} kernel (in Section III), in which the gradient acts on an orbital, involves the orbital–gradient product ϕp(𝐫)∇ϕq(𝐫)\phi_{p}({\bf r})\,\nabla\phi_{q}({\bf r}), we perform a second pivoted Cholesky on the diagonal

Dg(∇)=wg2​(∑pϕp​(𝐫g)2)​(∑p,c(∂cϕp​(𝐫g))2),D^{(\nabla)}_{g}=w_{g}^{2}\Big(\sum_{p}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})^{2}\Big)\!\Big(\sum_{p,c}\big(\partial_{c}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\big)^{2}\Big), (16)

with the corresponding column

Sg​g′(∇)=(∑pϕpw​(𝐫g)​ϕpw​(𝐫g′))​(∑p,c∂cϕpw​(𝐫g)​∂cϕpw​(𝐫g′)).S^{(\nabla)}_{gg^{\prime}}=\Big(\sum_{p}\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\Big)\Big(\sum_{p,c}\partial_{c}\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\partial_{c}\phi^{w}_{p}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\Big). (17)

Both production decompositions run to prescribed ranks Nμ(ϕ)N_{\mu}^{(\phi)} and Nμ(∇)N_{\mu}^{(\nabla)}; there is no residual-tolerance stopping criterion. The ranks are set from the chosen rank ratios and the two resulting pivot sets are subsequently fused. The decomposition itself is matrix-free (Section IV.2).

Pivot fusion.

We take the union of the two pivot sets as the final interpolation set, denote its cardinality by NμN_{\mu}, and relabel its points {𝐫μ}μ=1Nμ\{{\bf r}_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{N_{\mu}}. This forces the scalar and gradient auxiliary bases to share a single pivot index μ\mu, so that the pivot-point tensors Cqp​(𝐫μ)=ϕp​(𝐫μ)​ϕq​(𝐫μ)C^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu})=\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\mu})\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}) and 𝐂~qp(𝐫μ)=ϕp(𝐫μ)∇ϕq(𝐫μ)\tilde{\bf C}^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu})=\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\mu})\nabla\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}) appear simultaneously in the later contractions without any re-indexing or interpolation between incompatible pivot sets. Because the gradient pivots are largely distinct from the scalar ones, the fused set is roughly twice the size of a single channel, but every intermediate in the KK and Δ​U\Delta U assembly addresses a single auxiliary dimension.

Auxiliary basis fitting.

Given the fused pivots, ISDF approximates the densities as

ρqp​(𝐫)\displaystyle\rho^{p}_{q}({\bf r}) ≈∑μξμ​(𝐫)​Cqp​(𝐫μ),\displaystyle\approx\;\sum_{\mu}\xi_{\mu}({\bf r})\,C^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}), (18)
ϕp​(𝐫)​∂cϕq​(𝐫)\displaystyle\phi_{p}({\bf r})\,\partial_{c}\phi_{q}({\bf r}) ≈∑μξ~cμ(𝐫)C~p,cq(𝐫μ),c∈{x,y,z},\displaystyle\approx\;\sum_{\mu}\tilde{\xi}^{c}_{\mu}({\bf r})\,\tilde{C}^{p,c}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}),\qquad c\in\{x,y,z\},

where ξμ​(𝐫)\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}) and the component-specific ξ~μc​(𝐫)\tilde{\xi}_{\mu}^{c}({\bf r}) are determined by minimizing the Frobenius norm of the residual, following the least-squares fitting strategy first introduced for tensor hypercontraction[44] and later adopted for ISDF[25]. The associated normal equations

∑ν(C​C⊤)μ​ν​ξν​(𝐫)=∑p​qCqp​(𝐫μ)​ρqp​(𝐫),\sum_{\nu}(CC^{\top})_{\mu\nu}\,\xi_{\nu}({\bf r})=\sum_{pq}C^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,\rho^{p}_{q}({\bf r}), (19)

are solved directly through a Cholesky factorization of the dense Nμ×NμN_{\mu}\times N_{\mu} Gram matrix (C​C⊤)μ​ν=Gμ​ν2(CC^{\top})_{\mu\nu}=G_{\mu\nu}^{2}, where Gμ​ν=∑pϕp​(𝐫μ)​ϕp​(𝐫ν)G_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{p}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\mu})\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\nu}) (see Section IV.2 for the numerical safeguards). The gradient auxiliary basis ξ~μc\tilde{\xi}_{\mu}^{c} is obtained by solving the analogous system three times, one per Cartesian component, but with the mixed normal-equation matrix

(C~c​C~c⊤)μ​ν=(∑p∂cϕp​(𝐫μ)​∂cϕp​(𝐫ν))​(∑qϕq​(𝐫μ)​ϕq​(𝐫ν)),(\tilde{C}^{c}\tilde{C}^{c\top})_{\mu\nu}=\Big(\sum_{p}\partial_{c}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\mu})\partial_{c}\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{\nu})\Big)\Big(\sum_{q}\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu})\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{\nu})\Big), (20)

and a right-hand side formed from the corresponding gradient–scalar product at the target grid point. Thus the scalar auxiliary uses scalar–scalar pivot factors, whereas each Cartesian gradient auxiliary uses a gradient factor on one orbital index and a scalar factor on the other. Following traditional ISDF terminology we refer to ξ\xi and ξ~\tilde{\xi} as the auxiliary density and auxiliary gradient density, respectively.

Grid-batched streaming.

The tensors ξμ​(𝐫g)\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g}) and ξ~μ​(𝐫g)\tilde{\xi}_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g}) are the only objects whose storage grows with the dense grid size NgN_{g}. They are therefore evaluated in grid batches and, when necessary, streamed to disk rather than held in device or host memory. During integral assembly, batches are brought back to the device asynchronously by a depth-one prefetch mechanism, so that host-to-device transfer overlaps with compute.

III ISDF Representation of the TC Integrals

III.1 Two-body KK integrals

The real-space expression for the two-body correction in Ref. 11 separates naturally into three kernels:

Kr​sp​q​(1)\displaystyle K^{pq(1)}_{rs} =⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)|∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1|ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)⟩,\displaystyle=\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)|\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}|\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)}, (21)
Kr​sp​q​(2)\displaystyle K^{pq(2)}_{rs} =⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)|∇12​u​(1,2)|ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)⟩,\displaystyle=\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)|\nabla_{1}^{2}u(1,2)|\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)},
Kr​sp​q​(3)\displaystyle K^{pq(3)}_{rs} =⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)|(∇1u​(1,2))2|ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)⟩.\displaystyle=\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)|(\nabla_{1}u(1,2))^{2}|\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)}.

Collecting the three kernels with the symmetrization 𝒫^12\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}, the two-body kernel entering Eq. (4) is

Kr​sp​q=𝒫^12​[Kr​sp​q​(1)+12​Kr​sp​q​(2)+12​Kr​sp​q​(3)],K^{pq}_{rs}=\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\!\left[K^{pq(1)}_{rs}+\tfrac{1}{2}K^{pq(2)}_{rs}+\tfrac{1}{2}K^{pq(3)}_{rs}\right], (22)

with 𝒫^12​Tr​sp​q=Tr​sp​q+Ts​rq​p\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\,T^{pq}_{rs}=T^{pq}_{rs}+T^{qp}_{sr} denoting electron-1↔\leftrightarrow2 exchange, which simultaneously interchanges p↔qp\leftrightarrow q and r↔sr\leftrightarrow s in the physicists’ index convention used here. To avoid the numerically expensive Laplacian, we integrate by parts, a reformulation first used in the supplementary material of Ref. 11, to rewrite

Kr​sp​q​(2)\displaystyle K^{pq(2)}_{rs} =−⟨ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)|∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1|ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)⟩\displaystyle=-\,\Braket{\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)|\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}|\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)} (23)
−⟨ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)|∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1|ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)⟩,\displaystyle-\,\Braket{\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)|\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}|\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)},

which reduces K(2)K^{(2)} to two K(1)K^{(1)}-style evaluations with swapped orbital labels; the surface terms vanish for the localized square-integrable orbital products used here. Writing Kr​s(1,swap)​p​q=⟨ϕr​(1)​ϕs​(2)|∇1u​(1,2)⋅∇1|ϕp​(1)​ϕq​(2)⟩K^{(1,\mathrm{swap})pq}_{rs}=\Braket{\phi_{r}(1)\phi_{s}(2)|\nabla_{1}u(1,2)\cdot\nabla_{1}|\phi_{p}(1)\phi_{q}(2)} for the swapped contraction, so that K(2)=−K(1)−K(1,swap)K^{(2)}=-K^{(1)}-K^{(1,\mathrm{swap})}, Eq. (22) reduces to the form assembled in practice,

Kr​sp​q=12​𝒫^12​[Kr​sp​q​(1)−Kr​sp​q​(1,swap)+Kr​sp​q​(3)].K^{pq}_{rs}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\!\left[K^{pq(1)}_{rs}-K^{pq(1,\mathrm{swap})}_{rs}+K^{pq(3)}_{rs}\right]. (24)

We therefore discuss only K(1)K^{(1)} and K(3)K^{(3)} in what follows.

Substituting the ISDF factorizations in Eq. (18) yields

Kr​sp​q​(1)\displaystyle K^{pq(1)}_{rs} =∑g,g′wgwg′[ϕp(𝐫g)∇ϕr(𝐫g)]⋅∇u(𝐫g,𝐫g′)\displaystyle=\sum_{g,g^{\prime}}w_{g}w_{g^{\prime}}\,\big[\phi_{p}({\bf r}_{g})\,\nabla\phi_{r}({\bf r}_{g})\big]\!\cdot\!\nabla u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}) (25)
×ϕq​(𝐫g′)​ϕs​(𝐫g′)\displaystyle\times\phi_{q}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\phi_{s}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})
=∑μ​ν𝐮μ​ν(1)⋅𝐂~rp​(𝐫μ)​Csq​(𝐫ν),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\nu}{\bf u}^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}\!\cdot\!\tilde{\bf C}^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,C^{q}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}),

with the vector-valued Jastrow kernel (three Cartesian components)

uμ​ν(1),c\displaystyle u^{(1),c}_{\mu\nu} =∑g,g′wg​wg′​ξ~μc​(𝐫g)​ξν​(𝐫g′)​∂cu⁡(𝐫g,𝐫g′),\displaystyle=\sum_{g,g^{\prime}}w_{g}\,w_{g^{\prime}}\,\tilde{\xi}^{c}_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g})\,\xi_{\nu}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\,\partial_{c}u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}), (26)
𝐮(1)\displaystyle{\bf u}^{(1)} ∈ℝNμ×Nμ×3.\displaystyle\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mu}\times N_{\mu}\times 3}.

The analogous K(3)K^{(3)} expression reads

Kr​sp​q​(3)\displaystyle K^{pq(3)}_{rs} =∑μ​νuμ​ν(3)​Crp​(𝐫μ)​Csq​(𝐫ν),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\nu}u^{(3)}_{\mu\nu}\,C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,C^{q}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}), (27)
uμ​ν(3)\displaystyle u^{(3)}_{\mu\nu} =∑g,g′wg​wg′​ξμ​(𝐫g)​ξν​(𝐫g′)​(∇u​(𝐫g,𝐫g′))2,\displaystyle=\sum_{g,g^{\prime}}w_{g}w_{g^{\prime}}\,\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g})\,\xi_{\nu}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\,\big(\nabla u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\big)^{2},

where now u(3)∈ℝNμ×Nμu^{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mu}\times N_{\mu}} is scalar (no Cartesian component) because it contracts the squared gradient.

III.2 Effective two-body correction Δ​U\Delta U from xTC

Explicit evaluation of the rank-six LL tensor in Eq. (4) is prohibitive already for moderate system sizes. Following the xTC scheme of Ref. 10 we instead absorb LL into an effective two-body correction by contracting two of its three pairs with the Hartree–Fock one-particle reduced density matrix γtu=⟨at†​au⟩\gamma^{u}_{t}=\Braket{a_{t}^{\dagger}a_{u}}, defined here as the one-spin spatial-orbital density (occupied eigenvalues equal to one). We keep the physicists’ index convention used throughout the article: in Δ​Ur​sp​q\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}, the pairs (p,r)(p,r) and (q,s)(q,s) are the bra–ket orbital pairs of electron 1 and electron 2, respectively. The result is a sum of four contributions that, after inserting the ISDF factorizations (18), each take a form well suited to grid-batched contraction:

Δ​Ur​sp​q=−𝒫^12​[Term1+Term2+Term3+Term4],\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}=-\,\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\!\big[\,\mathrm{Term}_{1}+\mathrm{Term}_{2}+\mathrm{Term}_{3}+\mathrm{Term}_{4}\,\big], (28)

with the electron-1↔\leftrightarrow2 exchange 𝒫^12​Tr​sp​q=Tr​sp​q+Ts​rq​p\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}T^{pq}_{rs}=T^{pq}_{rs}+T^{qp}_{sr} acting as in Eq. (22), which enforces the particle-exchange relation Δ​Ur​sp​q=Δ​Us​rq​p\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}=\Delta U^{qp}_{sr}. To specify the four terms before applying ISDF, define the orbital-pair and density-matrix-contracted fields

ρba​(𝐫g)\displaystyle\rho^{a}_{b}({\bf r}_{g}) =ϕa​(𝐫g)​ϕb​(𝐫g),\displaystyle=\phi_{a}({\bf r}_{g})\phi_{b}({\bf r}_{g}), (29)
ργ​(𝐫g)\displaystyle\rho_{\gamma}({\bf r}_{g}) =∑t​uγtu​ρut​(𝐫g),\displaystyle=\sum_{tu}\gamma^{u}_{t}\rho^{t}_{u}({\bf r}_{g}),
βsu​(𝐫g)\displaystyle\beta^{u}_{s}({\bf r}_{g}) =∑tγtu​ρst​(𝐫g),\displaystyle=\sum_{t}\gamma^{u}_{t}\rho^{t}_{s}({\bf r}_{g}),
𝐀b,ga\displaystyle{\bf A}^{a}_{b,g} =∑g′wg′ρab(𝐫g′)∇u(𝐫g,𝐫g′),\displaystyle=\sum_{g^{\prime}}w_{g^{\prime}}\rho^{a}_{b}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\nabla u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}),
𝐀γ,g\displaystyle{\bf A}_{\gamma,g} =∑g′wg′ργ(𝐫g′)∇u(𝐫g,𝐫g′),\displaystyle=\sum_{g^{\prime}}w_{g^{\prime}}\rho_{\gamma}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\nabla u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}),
𝐁s,gu\displaystyle{\bf B}^{u}_{s,g} =∑g′wg′βus(𝐫g′)∇u(𝐫g,𝐫g′).\displaystyle=\sum_{g^{\prime}}w_{g^{\prime}}\beta^{u}_{s}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\nabla u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}).

The pre-ISDF contributions are then

Term1\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{1} =2​∑gwg​ρrp​(𝐫g)​𝐀γ,g⋅𝐀s,gq,\displaystyle=2\sum_{g}w_{g}\rho^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{g}){\bf A}_{\gamma,g}\!\cdot\!{\bf A}^{q}_{s,g}, (30)
Term2\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{2} =−∑gwgρpr(𝐫g)∑u𝐁us,g⋅𝐀qu,g,\displaystyle=-\sum_{g}w_{g}\rho^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{g})\sum_{u}{\bf B}^{u}_{s,g}\!\cdot\!{\bf A}^{q}_{u,g},
Term3\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{3} =−∑gwg𝐀pr,g⋅∑u[βus(𝐫g)𝐀qu,g+𝐁us,gρqu(𝐫g)],\displaystyle=-\sum_{g}w_{g}{\bf A}^{p}_{r,g}\!\cdot\!\sum_{u}\!\left[\beta^{u}_{s}({\bf r}_{g}){\bf A}^{q}_{u,g}+{\bf B}^{u}_{s,g}\rho^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{g})\right],
Term4\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{4} =∑gwg​ργ​(𝐫g)​𝐀r,gp⋅𝐀s,gq.\displaystyle=\sum_{g}w_{g}\rho_{\gamma}({\bf r}_{g}){\bf A}^{p}_{r,g}\!\cdot\!{\bf A}^{q}_{s,g}.

Throughout this section, μ,ν,λ\mu,\nu,\lambda label auxiliary (ISDF) indices, so that 𝐫μ{\bf r}_{\mu} denotes the corresponding pivot point; g,g′g,g^{\prime} label grid points, c∈{x,y,z}c\in\{x,y,z\} labels Cartesian components, α\alpha labels columns of the density projector, and p,q,r,s,t,up,q,r,s,t,u label MO indices. We keep the pivot-tensor notation of Eq. (18), writing scalar factors as Cqp​(𝐫μ)C^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}) and reserving 𝐂~qp​(𝐫μ)\tilde{\bf C}^{p}_{q}({\bf r}_{\mu}) for gradient factors. We pre-compute three orbital-independent intermediates,

Gν\displaystyle G_{\nu} =∑t​uCut​(𝐫ν)​γtu,\displaystyle=\sum_{tu}C^{t}_{u}({\bf r}_{\nu})\,\gamma^{u}_{t}, (31)
Ls​νu\displaystyle L^{u}_{s\nu} =∑tγtu​Cst​(𝐫ν),\displaystyle=\sum_{t}\gamma^{u}_{t}\,C^{t}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}),
𝒢μ,gc\displaystyle\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g} =∑g′wg′​ξμ​(𝐫g′)​∂cu⁡(𝐫g,𝐫g′).\displaystyle=\sum_{g^{\prime}}w_{g^{\prime}}\,\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g^{\prime}})\,\partial_{c}u({\bf r}_{g},{\bf r}_{g^{\prime}}).

Here GνG_{\nu} is the density matrix contracted against an ISDF vertex, Ls​νuL^{u}_{s\nu} is the corresponding density-dressed vertex with one open orbital pair, and 𝒢μ,gc\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g} is a grid-local gradient–interaction kernel encoding the action of ∇u\nabla u on the auxiliary basis. Inserting Eq. (18) into Eq. (29) gives the direct mapping

ργ​(𝐫g)\displaystyle\rho_{\gamma}({\bf r}_{g}) ≃∑λGλ​ξλ​(𝐫g),\displaystyle\simeq\sum_{\lambda}G_{\lambda}\xi_{\lambda}({\bf r}_{g}), 𝐀b,ga\displaystyle{\bf A}^{a}_{b,g} ≃∑μCba​(𝐫μ)​𝓖μ,g,\displaystyle\simeq\sum_{\mu}C^{a}_{b}({\bf r}_{\mu}){\bm{\mathcal{G}}}_{\mu,g}, (32)
βsu​(𝐫g)\displaystyle\beta^{u}_{s}({\bf r}_{g}) ≃∑νLs​νu​ξν​(𝐫g),\displaystyle\simeq\sum_{\nu}L^{u}_{s\nu}\xi_{\nu}({\bf r}_{g}), 𝐁s,gu\displaystyle{\bf B}^{u}_{s,g} ≃∑νLs​νu​𝓖ν,g.\displaystyle\simeq\sum_{\nu}L^{u}_{s\nu}{\bm{\mathcal{G}}}_{\nu,g}.

Thus Terms 1 and 4 generate the D(1)D^{(1)} and D(4)D^{(4)} kernels below, while Terms 2 and 3 generate X(2)X^{(2)} and X(3)X^{(3)}, respectively.

Terms 1 and 4 (factorizable).

Both terms reduce to a pure Nμ2N_{\mu}^{2} contraction, with dominant grid cost 𝒪⁡(Ng​Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}N_{\mu}^{2}):

Term4\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{4} =∑μ​νCrp​(𝐫μ)​Dμ​ν(4)​Csq​(𝐫ν),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\nu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,D^{(4)}_{\mu\nu}\,C^{q}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}), (33)
Dμ​ν(4)\displaystyle D^{(4)}_{\mu\nu} =∑gw~g​(∑c𝒢μ,gc​𝒢ν,gc),\displaystyle=\sum_{g}\tilde{w}_{g}\!\left(\sum_{c}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g}\right),
w~g\displaystyle\tilde{w}_{g} =wg​∑λGλ​ξλ​(𝐫g),\displaystyle=w_{g}\sum_{\lambda}G_{\lambda}\,\xi_{\lambda}({\bf r}_{g}),
Term1\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{1} =2​∑μ​νCrp​(𝐫μ)​Dμ​ν(1)​Csq​(𝐫ν),\displaystyle=2\sum_{\mu\nu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,D^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}\,C^{q}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}),
Dμ​ν(1)\displaystyle D^{(1)}_{\mu\nu} =∑gwg​ξμ​(𝐫g)​Vν,g,\displaystyle=\sum_{g}w_{g}\,\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g})\,V_{\nu,g},
Vν,g\displaystyle V_{\nu,g} =∑cHg​c𝒢cν,g,Hg​c=∑λGλ𝒢cλ,g.\displaystyle=\sum_{c}H_{gc}\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g},\quad H_{gc}=\sum_{\lambda}G_{\lambda}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\lambda,g}.

The intermediates D(4)D^{(4)} and D(1)D^{(1)} are of 𝒪⁡(Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mu}^{2}).

Terms 2 and 3 (non-factorizable).

These contributions retain one open orbital index inherited from the density matrix. Introducing

Ys,g,cu\displaystyle Y^{u}_{s,g,c} =∑νLs​νu​𝒢ν,gc,\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu}L^{u}_{s\nu}\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g}, (34)
Zu,g,cq\displaystyle Z^{q}_{u,g,c} =∑νCuq​(𝐫ν)​𝒢ν,gc,\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu}C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\nu})\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g},

one obtains

Term2\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{2} =−∑μCpr(𝐫μ)X(2)q​s​μ,\displaystyle=-\sum_{\mu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,X^{(2)}_{qs\mu}, (35)
Xq​s​μ(2)\displaystyle X^{(2)}_{qs\mu} =∑gwg​ξμ​(𝐫g)​∑u,cYs,g,cu​Zu,g,cq,\displaystyle=\sum_{g}w_{g}\,\xi_{\mu}({\bf r}_{g})\sum_{u,c}Y^{u}_{s,g,c}\,Z^{q}_{u,g,c},
Term3\displaystyle\mathrm{Term}_{3} =−∑μCpr(𝐫μ)X(3)q​s​μ,X(3)q​s​μ=X(3,1)q​s​μ+X(3,2)q​s​μ,\displaystyle=-\sum_{\mu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,X^{(3)}_{qs\mu},\quad X^{(3)}_{qs\mu}=X^{(3,1)}_{qs\mu}+X^{(3,2)}_{qs\mu},

with

Xq​s​μ(3,1)\displaystyle X^{(3,1)}_{qs\mu} =∑g,cwg​𝒢μ,gc​∑uL~s,gu​Zu,g,cq,\displaystyle=\sum_{g,c}w_{g}\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g}\sum_{u}\tilde{L}^{u}_{s,g}\,Z^{q}_{u,g,c}, (36)
L~s,gu\displaystyle\tilde{L}^{u}_{s,g} =∑νLs​νu​ξν​(𝐫g),\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu}L^{u}_{s\nu}\,\xi_{\nu}({\bf r}_{g}),
Xq​s​μ(3,2)\displaystyle X^{(3,2)}_{qs\mu} =∑g,cwg​𝒢μ,gc​∑uYs,g,cu​C^u,gq,\displaystyle=\sum_{g,c}w_{g}\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g}\sum_{u}Y^{u}_{s,g,c}\,\widehat{C}^{q}_{u,g},
C^u,gq\displaystyle\widehat{C}^{q}_{u,g} =∑νCuq​(𝐫ν)​ξν​(𝐫g).\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu}C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\nu})\,\xi_{\nu}({\bf r}_{g}).

The dominant grid cost of Terms 2–3 is 𝒪⁡(Ng​Nμ​Norb2)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}N_{\mu}N_{\rm orb}^{2}), set by the contraction over the open orbital index uu; the storage of the resulting intermediates and their disk staging are discussed in Section IV.3.

Low-rank projector for Terms 2 and 3.

A key algorithmic ingredient of our implementation is that the density-matrix contraction inside the exchange kernel can be applied through a low-rank projector. Observing that

∑u,cYs,g,cu​Zu,g,cq\displaystyle\sum_{u,c}Y^{u}_{s,g,c}\,Z^{q}_{u,g,c} =∑u,c∑μ,νLs​νu​𝒢ν,gc​Cuq​(𝐫μ)​𝒢μ,gc\displaystyle=\sum_{u,c}\sum_{\mu,\nu}L^{u}_{s\nu}\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g}\,C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\mu})\,\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g} (37)
=∑μ​ν[∑uLs​νu​Cuq​(𝐫μ)]​(∑c𝒢ν,gc​𝒢μ,gc),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\nu}\Big[\sum_{u}L^{u}_{s\nu}C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\mu})\Big]\!\Big(\sum_{c}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g}\Big),

the bracketed density contraction can be written in factored form by decomposing the reference density matrix as γ=LQ​LQ⊤\gamma=L_{Q}L_{Q}^{\top}, with LQL_{Q} the code-level low-rank projector:

∑uLs​νu​Cuq​(𝐫μ)\displaystyle\sum_{u}L^{u}_{s\nu}C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\mu}) =∑αPs​ν,α​Pq​μ,α,\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}P_{s\nu,\alpha}P_{q\mu,\alpha}, (38)
Ps​ν,α\displaystyle P_{s\nu,\alpha} =∑tCst​(𝐫ν)​(LQ)t​α,\displaystyle=\sum_{t}C^{t}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu})(L_{Q})_{t\alpha},
Pq​μ,α\displaystyle P_{q\mu,\alpha} =∑uCuq​(𝐫μ)​(LQ)u​α.\displaystyle=\sum_{u}C^{q}_{u}({\bf r}_{\mu})(L_{Q})_{u\alpha}.

For the closed-shell Hartree–Fock reference used here, γ\gamma is idempotent in the MO basis, so LQL_{Q} coincides with the density projector itself. The naive 𝒪⁡(Ng​Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}N_{\mu}^{2}) exchange contraction is thereby replaced by an 𝒪⁡(Ng​Nμ​Norb)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}N_{\mu}N_{\rm orb}) contraction; the measured speedup is reported in Section IV.2.

Final assembly.

Combining the four terms,

Dμ​ν≡Dμ​ν(4)+2​Dμ​ν(1),Xq​s​μ≡Xq​s​μ(2)+Xq​s​μ(3),D_{\mu\nu}\equiv D^{(4)}_{\mu\nu}+2D^{(1)}_{\mu\nu},\qquad X_{qs\mu}\equiv X^{(2)}_{qs\mu}+X^{(3)}_{qs\mu}, (39)

the final assembly is

ΔUp​qr​s=−𝒫^12[\displaystyle\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}=-\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{12}\!\Big[ ∑μ​νCrp​(𝐫μ)​Dμ​ν​Csq​(𝐫ν)\displaystyle\sum_{\mu\nu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})D_{\mu\nu}C^{q}_{s}({\bf r}_{\nu}) (40)
−∑μCpr(𝐫μ)Xq​s​μ].\displaystyle-\sum_{\mu}C^{p}_{r}({\bf r}_{\mu})X_{qs\mu}\Big].

The assembly scales as 𝒪⁡(Norb4​Nμ)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm orb}^{4}N_{\mu}) in work and produces 𝒪⁡(Norb4)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm orb}^{4}) CCSD-facing tensor blocks when those blocks are materialized—identical in logical size to the final contraction step of a conventional density-fitted ERI assembly—and dominates the end-to-end cost for large NorbN_{\rm orb}.

III.3 Assembly of the effective xTC Hamiltonian

The two-body kernels of the preceding sections deliver the corrections Kr​sp​qK^{pq}_{rs} and Δ​Ur​sp​q\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}. Contracting these against the closed-shell reference one-particle density matrix reduces the transcorrelated Hamiltonian to a standard zero-, one-, and two-body operator, which is the object handed to the coupled-cluster solver. It is convenient to collect the two-body correction into

Wr​sp​q≡−Kr​sp​q+Δ​Ur​sp​q,W^{pq}_{rs}\equiv-\,K^{pq}_{rs}+\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}, (41)

so that the effective two-body integrals are Vr​sp​q+Wr​sp​qV^{pq}_{rs}+W^{pq}_{rs}.

One-body correction and Fock operator.

A partial contraction of Δ​U\Delta U over the occupied orbitals defines the one-body increment

Δhp​q=−12∑o∈occ(2ΔUq​op​o−ΔUo​qp​o).\Delta h_{pq}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{o\in\mathrm{occ}}\big(2\,\Delta U^{po}_{qo}-\Delta U^{po}_{oq}\big). (42)

The effective one-body (Fock) operator adds to Δ​h\Delta h the mean-field contraction of the two-body correction WW over the occupied space,

fp​qxTC=Δ​hp​q+∑i∈occ(2​Wq​ip​i−Wi​qp​i),f^{\rm xTC}_{pq}=\Delta h_{pq}+\sum_{i\in\mathrm{occ}}\big(2\,W^{pi}_{qi}-W^{pi}_{iq}\big), (43)

comprising a Coulomb-type term (weight 22 for the closed shell) and an exchange-type term. This correction is added to the bare-Hamiltonian Fock matrix built from VV; because KK and Δ​U\Delta U are non-Hermitian, fxTCf^{\rm xTC} is stored without symmetrization.

Scalar constant.

The fully-contracted remainder is a scalar that shifts the reference energy,

ExTC0=−23∑i∈occΔhi​i+Enuc,E^{\rm xTC}_{0}=-\tfrac{2}{3}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{occ}}\Delta h_{ii}+E_{\rm nuc}, (44)

formed from the same one-body operator Δ​h\Delta h traced over the occupied orbitals, together with the nuclear repulsion EnucE_{\rm nuc}.

Assembled Hamiltonian.

The Hamiltonian handed to the solver retains the original one- and two-electron integrals, with the one-body part renormalized by Δ​h\Delta h and the two-body part xTC-corrected,

H¯xTC=E0xTC+(hp​q+Δ​hp​q)​ap†​aq+12​(Vr​sp​q−Kr​sp​q+Δ​Ur​sp​q)​ap†​aq†​as​ar,\bar{H}_{\rm xTC}=E^{\rm xTC}_{0}+\big(h_{pq}+\Delta h_{pq}\big)\,a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}+\tfrac{1}{2}\big(V^{pq}_{rs}-K^{pq}_{rs}+\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}\big)\,a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{s}a_{r}, (45)

where hp​qh_{pq} are the bare one-electron integrals and Δ​h\Delta h and E0xTCE^{\rm xTC}_{0} are given by Eqs. (42) and (44). From this H¯xTC\bar{H}_{\rm xTC} the coupled-cluster solver builds its reference Fock matrix in the usual closed-shell way; the xTC contribution to that Fock is fxTCf^{\rm xTC} of Eq. (43). Because KK and Δ​U\Delta U are non-Hermitian, all one- and two-body integrals are stored without symmetrization.

IV Implementation

IV.1 Integration with CCSD

The transformed one- and two-body integrals, h~p​q=hp​q+Δ​hp​q\tilde{h}_{pq}=h_{pq}+\Delta h_{pq} and V~r​sp​q=Vr​sp​q−Kr​sp​q+Δ​Ur​sp​q\tilde{V}^{pq}_{rs}=V^{pq}_{rs}-K^{pq}_{rs}+\Delta U^{pq}_{rs}, respectively, are supplied to a restricted CCSD solver adapted to the non-Hermitian transcorrelated Hamiltonian. The transformed two-body correction is −K+Δ​U-K+\Delta U. It preserves particle exchange, Wr​sp​q=Ws​rq​pW^{pq}_{rs}=W^{qp}_{sr}, but breaks the Hermitian pair-block relation Wr​sp​q=Wp​qr​sW^{pq}_{rs}=W^{rs}_{pq} and hence the bare ERI’s eight-fold symmetry. The solver therefore treats non-equivalent integral blocks as independent tensors rather than relating them by transposition. The one-body Fock matrix and the scalar constant are assembled as described in Section III.3; like the two-body blocks they are non-Hermitian and stored without symmetrization.

Although carrying the ISDF factorization directly through the CCSD amplitude equations can yield lower-scaling formulations, that reduction is not used in the present study. Here, ISDF is used to construct the transformed integral blocks, which are then supplied to a conventional projective CCSD contraction sequence, modified only as required to retain the independent non-Hermitian blocks described above. The factor-direct formulation now under development retains the full doubles-amplitude tensor but contracts its virtual indices sequentially with the ISDF factors, applies the central kernels in the resulting occupied-pair/interpolation-rank intermediates, and back-transforms sequentially. This avoids explicit construction of the four-virtual integral tensor and reduces the dominant contraction from nominal sixth- to fifth-order scaling, without introducing a separate factorization of the doubles amplitudes. Development and validation of this lower-scaling solver will be pursued in future work.

The complete non-equivalent block list, together with the block-by-block tiling, streaming, and on-the-fly (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) protocol, is given in Supporting Information Section .

IV.2 Numerical implementation notes

Correlator evaluation.

The one-electron term χ\chi is evaluated through the same ordered-pair interface as u2u_{2}, entering each ordered pair as χ⁡(𝐫i)/(N−1)\chi({\bf r}_{i})/(N-1); summing its derivative over j≠ij\neq i reconstructs ∇iχ​(𝐫i)\nabla_{i}\chi({\bf r}_{i}) exactly, so this evaluation is equivalent to the symmetric effective kernel of Eq. (2).

VMC numerics.

The fixed reference density |Φ0|2|\Phi_{0}|^{2} is sampled with Gaussian single-electron Metropolis–Hastings proposals and Sherman–Morrison determinant updates. The parameter-space dimension is modest for the BH correlator (typically Np≲100N_{\rm p}\lesssim 100), so the dense Gauss–Newton curvature matrix of Eq. (12) is stored and factorized directly.

Matrix-free pivot search.

The pivoted Cholesky selection of Section II.4 never materializes the orbital-pair matrix MM or the dense grid-by-grid Gram matrix SS. After a pivot g⋆g^{\star} is chosen, the new Cholesky column is Lg​μ=(Sg​g⋆−∑λ<μLg​λ​Lg⋆​λ)/dg⋆L_{g\mu}=(S_{gg^{\star}}-\sum_{\lambda<\mu}L_{g\lambda}L_{g^{\star}\lambda})/\sqrt{d_{g^{\star}}}, and the residual diagonal is updated as dg←dg−Lg​μ2d_{g}\leftarrow d_{g}-L_{g\mu}^{2}. Each iteration stores only the residual diagonal, the previously accepted Cholesky columns, and one newly generated column Sg​g⋆S_{gg^{\star}} computed from orbital values (and, for the gradient branch, orbital gradients) at the candidate pivot and all grid points. This keeps the pivot search linear in NgN_{g} per accepted pivot and avoids the Norb2​NgN_{\rm orb}^{2}N_{g} storage that an explicit orbital-pair matrix would require.

Auxiliary-fit robustness.

Should the Cholesky factorization of the fitting Gram matrix of Section II.4 fail due to near-singularity, a small adaptive Tikhonov shift is added to the diagonal and the decomposition is retried.

Measured impact of the low-rank projector.

In our benchmarks the low-rank projector of Section III yields roughly a five-fold end-to-end wall-clock speedup (up to nine-fold for the isolated QQ-matrix contraction) in a benchmark using Nch≈10​NorbN_{\rm ch}\approx 10\,N_{\rm orb} per channel (Nμ∼20​NorbN_{\mu}\sim 20\,N_{\rm orb} after fusion), while preserving agreement with the dense reference tensor to 𝒪⁡(10−10)\mathcal{O}(10^{-10}) relative Frobenius error.

IV.3 Multi-GPU pipeline and out-of-core storage

Scaling and memory management.

The kernels 𝐮(1){\bf u}^{(1)} and u(3)u^{(3)} are orbital-independent and assembled once. Their construction scales as 𝒪⁡(Ng2​Nμ)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}^{2}N_{\mu}) (using each auxiliary vector only once per grid pair) and storage is 𝒪⁡(Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mu}^{2}). The final assembly of the full four-index tensor in Eqs. (25)–(27) first contracts one auxiliary index at 𝒪⁡(Nμ2​Norb2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mu}^{2}N_{\rm orb}^{2}) cost and then contracts the remaining auxiliary index into the four open orbital indices at 𝒪⁡(Nμ​Norb4)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mu}N_{\rm orb}^{4}) cost. The latter is the dominant step whenever four-index CCSD-facing blocks are materialized. Those blocks have 𝒪⁡(Norb4)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm orb}^{4}) logical size, but production assembly streams panels of width BB in one orbital index, giving peak panel storage 𝒪⁡(B​Norb3)\mathcal{O}(BN_{\rm orb}^{3}) in addition to the 𝒪⁡(Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mu}^{2}) kernels rather than holding the full tensor in memory. By contrast, a direct dense grid evaluation of the same integrals without density fitting would scale as 𝒪⁡(Ng2​Norb2)\mathcal{O}(N_{g}^{2}N_{\rm orb}^{2}), carrying the full grid-pair sum into every orbital-pair contraction; the ISDF compression Norb2→NμN_{\rm orb}^{2}\!\to\!N_{\mu} (with NμN_{\mu} a small multiple of NorbN_{\rm orb}) and the removal of the dense grid index from the final tensors are what render the construction tractable. Thus the low-rank compression removes the dense grid dependence from the transcorrelated-kernel intermediates, while the final solver interface is still handled as tiled or streamed four-index data. To keep the peak working memory independent of NgN_{g}, we organize both grid sums as doubly-blocked loops over the bra and ket grid batches, and block the pivot-to-orbital contraction over the auxiliary index μ\mu; Jastrow derivatives are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation of the correlator at every grid-pair batch.

The asymptotic scaling in Table 3 hides a practical bottleneck: several blocks of Δ​U\Delta U are too large to hold in GPU memory. For an illustrative all-electron benzene-scale sizing case (Nocc=21N_{\rm occ}=21, Nvir≈200N_{\rm vir}\approx 200, double precision) the (o​v​v​v)(ovvv) and (v​o​v​v)(vovv) panels of Δ​U\Delta U are each about 1.31.3 GB and the dense (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) panel is about 1313 GB; by Nvir≈300N_{\rm vir}\approx 300, these grow to about 4.54.5 GB and 6565 GB, respectively. The (o​v​v​v)(ovvv) and (v​o​v​v)(vovv) panels are therefore staged to disk and, during CCSD, streamed back to device memory one orbital tile at a time, while the dense (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) panel is either contracted on the fly or, when a materialized (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) is required, staged to disk through the same pipeline. The exchange-kernel intermediate Xq​s​μ(2)X^{(2)}_{qs\mu} of Section III is disk-staged the same way: it carries 𝒪⁡(Norb2​Nμ)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm orb}^{2}N_{\mu}) storage, which for benzene at cc-pCV5Z (Norb=1200N_{\rm orb}=1200, Nμ≈26,000N_{\mu}\approx 26{,}000) would occupy ∼300\sim 300 GB in double precision, far exceeding device memory.

Symmetry exploitation.

The intermediate Xq​s​μX_{qs\mu} inherits the symmetry Xq​s​μ=Xs​q​μX_{qs\mu}=X_{sq\mu} of the underlying orbital pair (q,s)(q,s), because the gradient auxiliary basis enters only through the symmetric combination ∑c𝒢μ,gc​𝒢ν,gc\sum_{c}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\mu,g}\mathcal{G}^{c}_{\nu,g}. The orbital tiling therefore computes only the upper-triangular (q≤s)(q\leq s) panels and copies the lower-triangular panels by transposition, cutting the work and storage footprint on the non-factorizable terms roughly in half.

Out-of-core assembly.

Two distinct multi-GPU paths are used. During ISDF kernel construction, the dense grid dimension is sharded across devices; every device accumulates a partial kernel, and a collective sum combines those partial results. After the kernels are formed, four-index CCSD-facing orbital panels are independent: whole panels are assigned round-robin to individual GPUs and written through a bounded asynchronous queue, with no cross-device reduction between panels. Chunk-aligned on-disk datasets and the two execution paths are detailed in Supporting Information Section .

Memory-aware tile selection.

Given a user-supplied (or auto-detected) device-memory budget, the panel block size bpanelb_{\rm panel} is chosen by a binary search that fits the simultaneous peak workspace: the ISDF intermediate DD, the orbital tile of XX, the pivot tensor CC, and the current output tile. The same procedure selects the grid-batch size for the kernel computations so that the pipeline remains compute-bound on the device.

V Computational Details

All calculations were carried out with pytc release v0.1.0 (commit 09e0235), interfaced with PySCF[53, 54]; code and reproducibility scripts are linked in the Data and Code Availability statement. The transcorrelated integral construction and the coupled-cluster solver are implemented in JAX[9] in double precision throughout. The mean-field reference is restricted Hartree–Fock.

Grid and ISDF.

The production calculations use Becke partitioning, Treutler–Ahlrichs radial nodes, Lebedev angular grids, and PySCF level 2 pruning, a grid setting validated for transcorrelated integral evaluation in Ref. 21, whose convergence tests we adopt here. Interpolation points are obtained by pivoted Cholesky decomposition of the scalar (ϕ​ϕ\phi\phi) and gradient (ϕ∇ϕ\phi\nabla\phi) densities. We denote the prescribed rank of each channel by NchN_{\rm ch}, setting Nμ(ϕ)=Nμ(∇)≡Nch=12​NorbN_{\mu}^{(\phi)}=N_{\mu}^{(\nabla)}\equiv N_{\rm ch}=12\,N_{\rm orb}, and take the union of the two pivot sets. The final auxiliary dimension Nμ≡NfusedN_{\mu}\equiv N_{\rm fused} is listed in Table 4 and satisfies Nfused≈1.8N_{\rm fused}\approx 1.8\,– 2.2​Nch\,2.2\,N_{\rm ch}. The adequacy of this rank is established in Fig. 1.

Jastrow and VMC.

The correlator is a composite of a one-body nuclear-cusp factor and a Boys–Handy form with 1717 terms per nucleus type [Eqs. (6)–(7)], yielding on the order of 2020 free parameters for the hydrogen chain (one nucleus type) and 4040 for the molecular systems (two nucleus types). The parameters are optimized by reference-variance VMC as described in Section II.3; a warm-up/refinement protocol is used, and the production correlator is obtained by averaging the stationary tail of the refinement trajectory. Walker counts, step counts, learning rates, burn-in, and averaging-window details are collected in Supporting Information Section .

Coupled cluster.

The non-Hermitian transcorrelated integrals are passed to a restricted CCSD solver following the projective non-Hermitian transcorrelated coupled-cluster framework of Refs. 32, 50, 49 (maximum 100100 iterations, level shift 0.10.1), with the (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) block contracted on the fly. The rate-limiting (v​v​v​v)(vvvv) integral tiles feeding the T^2\hat{T}_{2} residual are assembled on the GPU through the same multi-device pipeline used for the ISDF construction, while the remaining amplitude-update contractions run on the host. For the largest benzene calculation (cc-pCV5Z, Norb=1200N_{\rm orb}=1200) the CCSD iterations ran on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs and reached practical convergence in ∼29{\sim}29 h.

Systems and hardware.

Table 4 collects the system sizes and ISDF ranks. The hydrogen-chain rows report the cc-pV5Z MP2NO production spaces used for the large-chain calculations and cutoff checks; the energy figures below retain explicit basis labels. Ethylene uses cc-pVTZ, and benzene uses the cc-pCVDZ, cc-pCVTZ, cc-pCVQZ, and cc-pCV5Z bases. Calculations were run on NVIDIA A100, H200, and B200 GPUs according to system size: the H10 and small molecular references used a single A100 or H200, the longer hydrogen chains (H20–H50) used single H200 or B200 devices, and the benzene cc-pCV5Z calculation used eight B200 GPUs.

VI Results

VI.1 Accuracy of the ISDF approximation

Because the entire scheme rests on a low-rank ISDF representation of the transcorrelated integrals, we first verify that this approximation is systematically convergent. We do not evaluate the full three-body LL tensor in the production calculations; the approximation being accelerated is therefore the established xTC Hamiltonian rather than a dense three-body transcorrelated reference. Prior work has benchmarked xTC and non-Hermitian transcorrelated solvers in molecular and strongly correlated settings, including transcorrelated N2 binding and dissociation curves[10, 49, 20, 33]; the convergence test here therefore isolates the additional ISDF truncation error introduced by the grid-based factorization. For ethylene (C2H4, cc-pVTZ, Norb=116N_{\rm orb}=116) with a VMC-optimized Boys–Handy Jastrow, Fig. 1 reports the ISDF-xTC-CCSD total-energy error as a function of the per-channel rank ratio Nch/NorbN_{\rm ch}/N_{\rm orb}, measured against an explicit dense (non-ISDF) transcorrelated reference evaluated with the same Jastrow and solver convention. The dense reference gives Etot=−78.4904432130E_{\rm tot}=-78.4904432130 Ha, while the highest ISDF rank shown (Nch=20​NorbN_{\rm ch}=20\,N_{\rm orb}) gives Etot=−78.4904435930E_{\rm tot}=-78.4904435930 Ha, differing by only 3.8×10−73.8\times 10^{-7} Ha (0.38​μ0.38~\muHa). The ISDF truncation error in the total energy falls below 11 mHa by Nch≈6​NorbN_{\rm ch}\approx 6\,N_{\rm orb} and is converged to <0.01<0.01 mHa by Nch=10​NorbN_{\rm ch}=10\,N_{\rm orb}. The lowest ratio shown (Nch=4​NorbN_{\rm ch}=4\,N_{\rm orb}) is under-resolved (error ∼18{\sim}18 mHa) because the more diffuse triple-zeta basis raises the numerical rank of the orbital-product densities. Since the ISDF pivots are selected from the orbital products alone (Alg. 1), independently of the correlator, alternative differentiable correlators can be used without changing the pivot-selection procedure. The rank-convergence benchmark shown here uses the Boys–Handy/nuclear-cusp correlator of the production calculations.

VI.2 Hydrogen chain in the thermodynamic limit

For the cc-pV5Z production orbital spaces summarized in Table 4, we use MP2 natural-orbital (MP2NO) truncations: the virtual space is rotated to the eigenbasis of the MP2 one-particle density matrix and truncated by natural-orbital occupation[12], retaining nkeep/Natom=10n_{\mathrm{keep}}/N_{\mathrm{atom}}=10 virtual natural orbitals per atom. A complementary route to reducing basis-set errors at small-basis cost is the additive reference correction of Hauskrecht et al.[22], which retains the small-basis xTC correlation energy while importing the reference contribution from a larger basis; here we instead work directly in the large basis with MP2NO-truncated virtual spaces. We first establish the accuracy of this truncation and how the cc-pV5Z data are obtained. Figure 2 shows the cc-pV5Z convergence test for H10 at r=1.4r=1.4 bohr, a representative short-side bound-region separation. This focused cutoff diagnostic uses nkeep=100,150,200n_{\rm keep}=100,150,200, whereas the binding-curve extrapolations in Fig. 3 below use 100,200,300100,200,300 at every separation; the two datasets serve different purposes and are fitted independently using the same inverse-count form. Increasing the cutoff from 10 to 15 and 20 retained virtuals per atom changes the energy by only 0.0510.051 and 0.0250.025 mHa/atom, respectively. Because cc-pV5Z has a finite virtual space (nvir=544n_{\rm vir}=544 for H10), the physical full-virtual limit lies at the finite abscissa 1/(nvir/Natom)=10/544≈0.0181/(n_{\rm vir}/N_{\mathrm{atom}})=10/544\approx 0.018 rather than at the origin; evaluating the linear fit in 1/(nkeep/Natom)1/(n_{\mathrm{keep}}/N_{\mathrm{atom}}) there places the full-virtual cc-pV5Z limit within 0.0050.005 mHa/atom of the MRCI+Q+F12 reference, essentially coincident with the full-virtual cc-pVQZ result (+0.008+0.008 mHa/atom). The extrapolated 5Z and QZ full-virtual energies thus agree to ∼0.003{\sim}0.003 mHa/atom, indicating that cc-pVQZ is already essentially at the basis-set limit for this system. The finite nkeep/Natom=10n_{\mathrm{keep}}/N_{\mathrm{atom}}=10 production cutoff is within about 0.120.12 mHa/atom of that extrapolated limit, well below the 11 mHa/atom scale used in the chain benchmarks. Because only three cutoff points enter this empirical inverse-count fit, its intercept has no independent statistical error estimate and can retain fit-form bias; the quoted sub-mHa comparisons diagnose the selected linear extrapolation rather than establish sub-mHa certainty in the full-virtual limit.

With the MP2NO truncation validated, Fig. 3 compares xTC-CCSD and canonical CCSD at the cc-pVTZ, cc-pVQZ, and cc-pV5Z levels against an accurate MRCI+Q+F12 reference [41]; for xTC-CCSD the cc-pV5Z curve is obtained from the MP2NO series exactly as established above. Canonical CCSD remains well above the reference at every basis—1.31.3–2.32.3 mHa/atom at cc-pVQZ and still ∼1.1{\sim}1.1–1.51.5 mHa/atom even at the full cc-pV5Z basis—whereas xTC-CCSD lies within 0.60.6 mHa/atom at cc-pVTZ over r=1.2r=1.2–2.82.8 bohr and, over the central bound region r=1.4r=1.4–2.42.4 bohr, agrees with the reference to within 0.10.1 mHa/atom at cc-pVQZ—comparable to the reference’s own extrapolation uncertainty. Over the broader 1.21.2–2.82.8 bohr window, xTC-CCSD at cc-pVTZ already surpasses canonical CCSD at cc-pV5Z. This rapid convergence motivates retaining the cc-pVTZ thermodynamic-limit series as a lower-cost reference trend, with the residual basis and virtual-orbital cutoff error quantified by the cc-pV5Z MP2NO diagnostic above.

We benchmark ISDF-xTC-CCSD on the linear hydrogen chain, a canonical strongly-correlated model, over a range of interatomic separations r=1.4r=1.4–2.82.8 bohr. The upper end of this range reflects the domain where the single-reference, non-Hermitian CCSD solver converges robustly for these transcorrelated chains; more stretched geometries require a multireference treatment beyond the present solver. For the TDL series plotted here, each rr uses finite chains of N=20N=20, 3030, 4040, and 5050 atoms in the cc-pVTZ basis; we extrapolate the total energy per atom to the thermodynamic limit (TDL) by a linear least-squares fit in 1/N1/N, Etot​(N)/N=ETDL+a/NE_{\rm tot}(N)/N=E_{\rm TDL}+a/N (the per-separation fits are collected in the Supporting Information, Fig. ). Residual and fit-form sensitivity checks are reported there; they support the headline 11 mHa/atom comparison while cautioning against overinterpreting differences of a few tenths of a mHa. The extrapolated TDL energies are compared with the AFQMC+Δ\DeltaDMRG reference data of Motta et al. [41], alongside the LR-DMC(LDA), RCCSD, and RCCSD(T) results from the same compilation[41] (Fig. 4). Across all separations studied, ISDF-xTC-CCSD agrees with the reference to within ±1\pm 1 mHa/atom, a substantial improvement over canonical RCCSD, whose deviation approaches 22 mHa/atom near equilibrium. It matches the accuracy of RCCSD(T) and LR-DMC(LDA) while retaining the 𝒪⁡(N6)\mathcal{O}(N^{6}) cost of CCSD, avoiding both the 𝒪⁡(N7)\mathcal{O}(N^{7}) perturbative-triples step of RCCSD(T) and the stochastic sampling of the diffusion Monte Carlo references. An analogous TDL series in the cc-pV5Z basis with the MP2NO cutoff nkeep/Natom=10n_{\mathrm{keep}}/N_{\mathrm{atom}}=10 (open stars in Fig. 4; per-separation fits in Fig.  and Table  of the Supporting Information) reduces the maximum absolute reference deviation from 0.630.63 to 0.310.31 mHa/atom and supports residual orbital-basis effects below about 0.60.6 mHa/atom over this range at the stated MP2NO cutoff.

VI.3 Ground-state energy of benzene

Figure 5 shows the basis-set convergence of the benzene energy relative to the CBS Hartree–Fock limit, Δ​EHF,CBS=E−EHF,CBS\Delta E_{\rm HF,CBS}=E-E_{\rm HF,CBS}, across the cc-pCVXXZ series. At finite XX this quantity is not the conventional basis-specific correlation energy E​(X)−EHF​(X)E(X)-E_{\rm HF}(X); only its CBS limit equals the CBS correlation energy. Extrapolating to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit, ISDF-xTC-CCSD recovers Ecorr,CBS≈−1.418E_{\rm corr,CBS}\approx-1.418 EhE_{\rm h}, which lies between the canonical CCSD (≈−1.379\approx-1.379 EhE_{\rm h}) and CCSD(T) (≈−1.440\approx-1.440 EhE_{\rm h}) CBS values [46]: about 3939 mHa more correlation than CCSD, but still roughly 2222 mHa short of the CCSD(T)/CBS benchmark. It closely matches the three-layer FermiNet variational Monte Carlo (VMC) result (≈−1.417\approx-1.417 EhE_{\rm h}) [46]; the deeper four-layer VMC (≈−1.426\approx-1.426 EhE_{\rm h}) and the fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) FermiNet results (≈−1.436\approx-1.436 and −1.440-1.440 EhE_{\rm h} for the three- and four-layer ansätze) recover progressively more correlation, the four-layer FermiNet-DMC essentially reaching the CCSD(T)/CBS benchmark [46]. Since xTC introduces no explicit triples, this CCSD-level method captures about 64%64\% of the CCSD-to-CCSD(T) CBS gap (3939 of 6161 mHa) at the formal scaling of CCSD, without a perturbative-triples step or explicitly correlated neural-network ansätze such as the Psiformer [57]. Beyond the CBS value itself, transcorrelation makes the extrapolation markedly more robust to the choice of fit form: the exponential and inverse-power extrapolations of the xTC-CCSD correlation energy agree to 1.11.1 mHa, whereas for canonical CCSD and CCSD(T) they differ by 7.67.6 and 8.08.0 mHa, respectively. Each CBS value is a three-parameter fit to the three points (cc-pCVTZ/QZ/5Z), so this spread quantifies the sensitivity to the fit form, not a statistical uncertainty; the fit forms and fitted parameters are tabulated in the Supporting Information. The smoother, accelerated basis-set convergence of the transcorrelated correlation energy renders the extrapolated CBS limit far less sensitive to the extrapolation scheme.

Figure 6 reports the wall-clock time required to build the ISDF-xTC intermediates for benzene on a single B200 GPU across the cc-pCVXXZ (X=X= D, T, Q, 5) series, spanning Norb=138N_{\rm orb}=138 to 12001200. The setup time scales empirically as T⁡[s]≈0.030​Norb1.76T\,[\mathrm{s}]\approx 0.030\,N_{\rm orb}^{1.76} over this range, below the formal 𝒪⁡(Norb2​Nμ2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\rm orb}^{2}N_{\mu}^{2}) worst case; we emphasize that this is a three-point power-law fit over the accessible range rather than an asymptotic scaling result, with the largest cc-pCV5Z calculation (Norb=1200N_{\rm orb}=1200, Nfused=25894N_{\rm fused}=25894) completing in ≈2.3\approx 2.3 h. Here “setup” starts with grid/orbital preparation and includes the fixed-rank ISDF decomposition and the KK/Δ​U\Delta U kernel/intermediate construction. It excludes SCF, VMC optimization and history loading, four-index CCSD-facing block materialization, and the CCSD iterations.

VII Conclusions

We have presented an ISDF construction of the transcorrelated Hamiltonian for general differentiable Jastrow correlators. The method evaluates the transcorrelated integrals on a real-space grid, compresses the orbital-pair and orbital-gradient densities into a low-rank ISDF form, and combines this with the xTC reduction of the three-body operator to an effective two-body correction. Because the compact auxiliary dimension NμN_{\mu} (a small multiple of NorbN_{\rm orb}) replaces both the dense grid index NgN_{g} in the final integral tensors and the orbital-pair count Norb2N_{\rm orb}^{2} in the kernel intermediates, this lowers grid-dependent storage and integration costs by orders of magnitude relative to dense grid evaluation while retaining the flexibility of numerical integration. Automatic differentiation supplies Jastrow gradients, and an out-of-core GPU producer/consumer pipeline makes the construction tractable for hundreds of orbitals and large basis sets.

The ISDF approximation is systematically convergent: for ethylene in a triple-zeta basis the ISDF truncation error in the total energy falls well below 11 mHa by a per-channel rank ratio Nch/Norb≈10N_{\rm ch}/N_{\rm orb}\approx 10—with the production setting Nch=12​NorbN_{\rm ch}=12\,N_{\rm orb} comfortably converged. On the linear hydrogen chain, transcorrelation strongly accelerates basis-set convergence: xTC-CCSD at the triple-zeta level already surpasses canonical CCSD at quintuple-zeta over r=1.2r=1.2–2.82.8 bohr, and the thermodynamic-limit energies agree with AFQMC+Δ\DeltaDMRG references to within 11 mHa/atom across a wide range of bond lengths. For benzene, the method recovers a complete-basis-set correlation energy well beyond that of canonical CCSD and comparable to neural-network variational Monte Carlo, while remaining tractable up to cc-pCV5Z. In both cases transcorrelation substantially improves the accuracy of an otherwise approximate coupled-cluster treatment, recovering—at the formal scaling of CCSD—a substantial part of the correlation energy that conventionally requires perturbative triples or a considerably larger basis.

Natural next steps include periodic systems[52], pseudopotentials for heavier elements[51], higher-order coupled-cluster treatments of the transcorrelated Hamiltonian[40], stochastic treatments (e.g. AFQMC), and alternative or neural-network Jastrow forms. More broadly, the combination of automatically differentiable correlators with low-rank, GPU-accelerated integral construction makes the transcorrelated method a practical route to high accuracy in compact basis sets across a range of downstream solvers, from coupled cluster to stochastic and tensor-network approaches.

Data and Code Availability

The numerical data plotted in all figures, together with the plotting scripts that reproduce them, are available in the repository https://github.com/nickirk/tc-isdf-data. The pytc code used to produce these results is available at https://github.com/nickirk/pytc (release v0.1.0, commit 09e0235; also distributed as pytc-qc 0.1.0 on PyPI).
